title: It Runs in the Family
full_review:
Three generations of fathers and sons explore the foibles and follies of life and love in the pleasantly affecting serio-comedy, "It Runs in the Family" (MGM).

Directed by Fred Schepisi, the on-screen chemistry of Tinseltown father-son combo Kirk and Michael Douglas facilitates the theme of reconciliation to emerge with emotional honesty despite the at times schmaltzy sentimentality of the narrative.

The dramedy charts the ebb and flow of the Gromberg family, whose members' professional prosperity is in inverse proportion to their ability to communicate with each other.

Heading the dysfunctional clan is Mitchell Gromberg (Kirk Douglas), the hoary patriarch and retired founding partner of a prestigious New York law firm. Having recently suffered a stroke -- a narrative element resonating with the elder Douglas -- he has begun to ponder his own mortality.

His workaholic son, Alex (Michael Douglas), a highly successful corporate attorney with a penchant for social activism, finds himself knee-deep in his own existential crisis -- though of the midlife, rather than end-of-life, variety.

To his dismay, he realizes that when it comes to parenting, the rotten apple has not fallen far from the tree. While both men were more-than-adequate providers, neither bothered to read the rest of the job description. In addition to being a lousy father, Alex isn't scoring too high in the husband department either, having cheated on his wife (Bernadette Peters) with a fellow soup-kitchen volunteer.

The most recent links in the dysfunctional chain are Alex's two sons -- Asher (Cameron Douglas), a philandering, rudderless rebel, and Eli (Rory Culkin), a precocious 11-year-old, the most levelheaded of the lot. The performance of Cameron, Michael's real-life son, marks the first production to boast three generations in the same film; also included in the family affair is Kirk's former wife, Diana Douglas, who plays his on-screen spouse, Evelyn.

When Evelyn unexpectedly dies, the facade of civility collapses -- a devastating blow to the family's tenuous tethers. Much more than Mitchell's emotional rock, Evelyn served as a peacemaker between the warring kin. Her passing and Mitchell's subsequent mourning play as some of the most tender, emotionally honest scenes in the film -- serving as poignant reminders to savor times shared with loved ones.

When Mitchell calls a truce and offers conciliatory gestures, Alex is at a loss, his father-son musculature having atrophied through years of disuse. This spirit of detente, however, filters into Alex's relationship with his own sons -- especially the wayward Asher, whose nose-diving grades and campus drug dealing are setting him on the fast track to disaster.

Predictably, the Gromberg men close ranks, make amends and gain a deeper appreciation for each other. This, of course, is not accomplished without much intergenerational sarcasm and the obligatory teary-eyed reconciliation. However, the film's theme of forgiveness, as well as the pro-family message it espouses, make these saccharine moments easy pills to swallow -- even to applaud.

Early in the film, the Grombergs celebrate a raucous Passover Seder meal. While some may find the incessant squabbling and irreverent banter of the scene off-putting, it is refreshing to see a family -- however dysfunctional -- gather together to pray. This is laudable, taking into account Hollywood's aversion to include traditional religious practices for any purpose other than mockery. Typically, families like the Grombergs -- hip, educated and progressive -- are portrayed as religiously neutral, if not openly critical and hostile.

Due to recurring drug abuse and sexual situations, as well as minimal vulgarities and an instance of rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
